findings.title: Unstable Python hash() used for shared cache key
findings.body: The eligibility cache key is built with hash(tuple(sorted(snuba_params.project_ids))). Python documents hash() as unstable across processes and versions (hash randomization), so the same project set maps to different keys in different workers/restarts. Since the cache is shared (memcached/Redis), cross-process lookups miss and each process creates its own key for the same projects, defeating the 60s caching and bloating the cache. Use a stable encoding such as comma-joined sorted IDs or hashlib.

findings.title: 60-second eligibility cache returns stale upsampling decisions
findings.body: is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects caches allowlist eligibility (True/False) for 60 seconds keyed only by org and projects. If the project allowlist changes, queries for up to 60s use the old decision and return raw count() when scaled upsampled_count() was required or vice versa, with errors scaled by 1/sample_rate (e.g. 10x). The invalidate_upsampling_cache helper defined in the same file is never called in the PR, so there is no invalidation path.

findings.title: Upsampling check uses outer dataset instead of executed scoped_dataset
findings.body: _get_event_stats receives scoped_dataset, the dataset actually queried. The dashboard-split logic calls it with different datasets (scoped_dataset vs discover for errors-only and transactions-only subqueries). The eligibility check passes the outer dataset closed over from get(), not scoped_dataset, so an errors-only subquery run on discover can be judged as a metrics/transactions query and skip upsampling, or a transaction query can be judged as errors and get upsampled, returning wrong counts.

findings.title: Error-focus check reads original HTTP query and only matches event.type:error
findings.body: _is_error_focused_query inspects request.GET.get("query"), the original HTTP parameter, not the query string argument actually sent to Snuba. Dashboard-split code re-executes _get_event_stats with rewritten queries like (query) AND !event.type:transaction for errors and (query) AND event.type:transaction for transactions while request.GET is unchanged. The check also only matches substring event.type:error, so a discover errors-only query built from !event.type:transaction is treated as non-error and undercounts, while a transactions-only subquery issued when the HTTP query contained event.type:error is treated as error and sums sample_weight which does not exist for transactions.

findings.title: upsampled_count sums nullable sample_weight without fallback and truncates
findings.body: The new Discover function is toInt64(sum(sample_weight)) with no null handling. Any error row without sample_weight (events written before sampling, backfills, mixed data) contributes 0/NULL instead of 1, so buckets undercount and can collapse to 0. toInt64 also truncates fractional weights, so a rate that does not evenly divide 1 (e.g. 0.33 -> weight ~3.03) is systematically biased low on every bucket. It should sum coalesced weights with rounding, e.g. sum(ifNull(sample_weight, 1)).

findings.title: Internal upsampled_count function exposed as public API
findings.body: SnQLFunction upsampled_count is registered without private=True, unlike neighboring internal aggregates. That makes upsampled_count() directly queryable by any Discover user. Because it sums the internal sample_weight column, callers can invoke it on non-allowlisted projects or datasets where the column is missing or 1 and receive misleading scaled numbers, and can probe internal sampling state. Internal upsampling helpers should be private.

findings.title: Test factory blindly trusts client-supplied sample rate
findings.body: _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling copies client-controlled contexts.error_sampling.client_sample_rate into normalized_data[sample_rate] with no validation. It uses if client_sample_rate so rate 0 is dropped, swallows all errors with bare except pass, overwrites any existing sample_rate, and accepts out-of-range or non-numeric values. Tests built on it therefore validate upsampling against arbitrary client-supplied weights (a client sending 0.001 would inflate counts 1000x) that production ingestion must reject, making endpoint tests unrealistic and hiding a trust-boundary issue.

findings.title: Column transform only handles exact count() and hardcodes alias
findings.body: transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling only rewrites a column whose lowercased stripped value equals exactly count(). Variants such as count() as foo, count_if, count_unique, or equations containing count() are left as raw counts, so a request mixes raw and scaled series in one response. When it does match it forces upsampled_count() as count, discarding the caller's alias and injecting AS syntax into RPC y_axes paths that expect bare aggregates, risking validation failures or mislabeled series.

findings.title: Main upsampling entry point and cache behavior untested
findings.body: The test class exercises only private helpers (_are_all_projects_error_upsampled, transform, _is_error_focused_query, _should_apply_sample_weight_transform) and never calls the public is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects. Cache-key construction, 60s staleness, hash instability, and dataset/request interaction therefore have zero unit coverage, and the SnubaParams fixture with start=None/end=None is never used, so the caching bugs shipped in this PR cannot be caught.
